 Truths and Lies - Week 9
 By Steve 
 Schwarz | 11/4/26 
 The injury bug continues to haunt fantasy owners. Lamar Jackson 
 just came back from a high ankle sprain and lasted one play. Bhayshul 
 Tuten had a great Week 8, but now appears to be dealing with ankle 
 and foot issues. Matthew Stafford was seen leaving the stadium with 
 an ice pack on his throwing shoulder. Jeremiyah Love has anew ankle 
 injury, the Ravens will be starting a third quarterback and a new 
 placekicker and we all know that Christian Watson will try to play 
 in Week 9 with a cracked rib. I can foresee a distant future with 
 robot players. 
 Byes: Pittsburgh, Tennessee
 Truths
 "When you want to help people, you tell them the truth. 
 When you want to help yourself, you tell them what they want to 
 hear." - Thomas Sewell 
 1) Baker Mayfield completed zero passes against Atlanta, yet 
 his QB Rating was higher than his opponent.
 True. Mayfield didn't throw an interception, was sacked once, rushed 
 for 14 yards and lost two fumbles for a 39.6 rating. Meanwhile, 
 Michael 
 Penix Jr. went 8-for-24 for 125 yards, four interceptions, rushed 
 for 11 yards and fumbled once for a 12 QB Rating. The previous time 
 a quarterback won a game with zero completions in the Super Bowl 
 Era was September 29, 1974 when Joe Ferguson went 0-for-2 in a 16-12 
 win over the New York Jets. He beat Joe Namath, who went 2-for-18 
 for 33 yards and three interceptions. 
 2) Derrick Henry has become Lamar Jackson dependent.
 At least for 2026, this appears to be the case. In the first four 
 games of the season, with Lamar 
 Jackson under center, Henry has averaged 22.7 FPts/G with seven 
 touchdowns. In games without Jackson (I'm including Week 8 when 
 Jackson was in for just one pass play and injured his throwing hand), 
 he's averaging 11.5 FPts/G with two touchdowns. In three of four 
 games last season he scored under 20 fantasy points without Jackson. 
 It might not be too late to trade him to someone who thinks the 
 team will feature Henry without a good quarterback under center, 
 but in truth, Henry needs the threat of a passing game.
 3) Chase Brown was a slow starter last season, so no need 
 to think about selling.
 Through seven games last season, Brown averaged 9.8 FPts/G, but 
 turned it around at mid-season and averaged 21.2 FPts/G the remainder 
 of the year. So far in 2026, through seven games, he's averaging 
 13.6 FPts/G. I particularly like his 29 targets over the last four 
 games. His issue is getting into the end zone. To date, he's 
 scored just once. He scored 11 times in 2025, 10 times from game 
 No.8 to the end of the season. Sound familiar? Now is the time to 
 buy shares of Brown, not sell! 
 4) It might be time to sell high on Tony Pollard.
 Tony just produced the most fantasy points of his career, off 
 a 25-129-3 and 3-26-0 effort against the Bengals. That's 
 a fantastic 36.5 fantasy points! He's had his two best games 
 of the season while his backup, Tyjae Spears , is out with a knee 
 injury. The bad news is that the Titans are on bye this week which 
 gives Spears two weeks to heal. Additionally, when the team returns 
 in Week 10, they will play the Jaguars in two of the next three 
 games and Jacksonville is tough on running backs (ranked second 
 in fewest RB fantasy points allowed in 2026). That likely means 
 he isn't going to help you in three of the next four weeks. 
 If you can make the playoffs without him being great, then he 
 has a solid fantasy playoff schedule, but if you need to fight 
 to get into the playoffs, it might be a good time to sell. 
 5) You can never truly trust rookies.
 A perfect example comes from Omar Cooper Jr. 's Week 8 results. 
 He ran 26 routes (74%) and managed to produce zero targets. This 
 after back-to-back 100-yard days and 22.3 and 22.5 fantasy points 
 in Week 6 and Week 7, respectively. Third-year wideout Adonai Mitchell also ran 26 routes, but saw nine targets, seven receptions 
 for 142 yards and a score worth 27.2 fantasy points. Depending 
 on rookies takes a strong heart. Even the great Randy Moss, in 
 his rookie season (69-1,313-17), produced games of 2-14-0 and 
 1-6-0.
 Lies 
 "Repetition does not transform a lie into the truth." 
 – Franklin D. Roosevelts 1) D'Andre Swift is 
 having a great 2026, which if he continues, might end up being 
 the best in Bears history.
 False. With three touchdown runs on Monday night in Week 8, he's 
 up to 10 touchdowns which leads the NFL. He needs four touchdowns 
 in the next six games to match the totals of Walter Payton (1977, 
 1979) and Gale Sayers (1965). Does that mean I think Swift is 
 in a class with those two Hall of Fame running backs? No, just 
 better opportunities to score. Swift already has as many attempts 
 from inside the 5-yard line as Payton had for the entire season 
 in both years (15). Sorry, I couldn't find red zone statistics 
 for the amazing Sayers in his 1965 rookie season, but of his 22 
 total touchdowns that season (14 rushing, six receiving, two kick 
 returns), only two came from inside the 5-yard line. The "Kansas 
 Comet" also famously produced six touchdowns on one muddy 
 December day against the San Francisco 49ers (four rushing, one 
 receiving and one punt return).
 Swift is having a top-10 fantasy season, but he's not Payton 
 or Sayers.
 2) In the five games Patrick Surtain II has started in 2026, 
 Denver is allowing opposing QBs 23 fantasy points-a-game while 
 in the three games he missed, they allowed just 16.8.
 Here is proof that statistics can lie. To see why, all you need 
 to do is look at the quarterbacks the team faced in each group. 
 The five quarterbacks faced with PS2 were; Trevor Lawrence , Matthew Stafford , Brock Purdy and Patrick Mahomes twice. In the three 
 games he missed, the quarterbacks were Jacoby Brissett , Justin 
 Herbert and Sam Darnold .
 3) You want more proof that numbers and small sample sizes can 
 mislead you? 
 Tetairoa McMillan is averaging 45.2 FPts/G in games this season 
 without Jalen Coker and 10.6 FPts/G in the five games they have 
 played together. Coker missed out on the fun against the weak 
 Detroit Lions secondary and McMillan went off for 45.2 points. 
 In 2025, there were six games without Coker and McMillan averaged 
 12.8 and 11 games together he averaged 12.4. Always beware of 
 small sample-size statistics.
 4) You should still have confidence in George Pickens.
 I'm going to have to say no here. Pickens is down 4.1 FPts/G 
 from a season ago. And it's not due to drastic drop in targets. 
 He averaged 8.1 targets last season and he's a 7.8 this 
 season even after seeing just four in Week 8. Last season he produced 
 seven games of 17 fantasy points or more (41.2%), this season 
 just once in eight tries (12.5%). Worse yet, No.3 receiver Ryan Flournoy is getting more work and he's up from 3.5 targets 
 in 2025 to 5.5 targets. Additionally, the team has made a concerted 
 effort to run the ball more since the Green Bay game when Dak Prescott threw 54 passes (versus 13 rushing attempts by running 
 backs). In the two games since then, the Cowboys have passed 56 
 times and running backs have run the ball 68 times. The opportunities 
 are just not there for Pickens as they were in 2025.
 5) I still believe in DK Metcalf.
 Sorry, no. I don't believe Aaron Rodgers does either and 
 that's more of a concern. Metcalf has three receptions on 
 12 targets over the past two games. It appears that most of the 
 time it's after Rodgers has looked elsewhere first, saw 
 nothing open, then fired toward Metcalf in a last ditch effort. 
 His last 17 receptions have accounted for just 165 yards and zero 
 scores, including one catch of 51 yards, meaning 16 catches averaged 
 7.1 ypr. Over the last four games, rookie Germie Bernard has seen 
 31 targets, 25 receptions for 224 yards and a score. I like Bernard 
 better the rest of the way.
